concept.name: Falling wedge
concept.definition: A technical-analysis pattern in which price makes lower highs and lower lows but both bounding trend lines slope downward and converge, compressing the decline. It is conventionally read as bullish: the converging lines show the sell-off losing momentum, with resolution expected through a break above the upper trend line — as a reversal after a downtrend or as a continuation pause within an uptrend. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Sellers keep pushing price down, but each new low is harder to achieve — selling pressure is exhausting, and the spring typically releases upward through the upper line.
concept.mechanics: Draw two downward-sloping, converging trend lines through at least two highs and two lows; volume typically contracts during formation. The trigger is a break above the upper trend line, ideally with volume expansion; the wedge's convergence allows a relatively close stop-loss below the pattern, which is why traders value its reward-to-risk geometry.
concept.failure_modes: In persistent bear markets a falling wedge can resolve downward (a downside break of the lower line continues the decline), and in rotating, trendless markets the pattern loses efficacy. As with all trend-line patterns, anchor selection is subjective.
concept.misconceptions: That the falling wedge's bullish label means buy immediately — the signal is only the upside break of the upper line; buying inside the falling range is catching a falling knife. It is also frequently confused with a descending triangle, whose bottom line is horizontal.
concept.example: A stock slides from $60 to $48 with each new low only slightly under the prior one and volume drying up; a close above the falling upper trend line at $51 marks the bullish resolution.
